title: Show us the Father (John 14:8–21)
hook: Philip asks, and he says: whoever has seen me has seen the Father

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rooms in the Father's house, and a table where the friends were troubled. Your line was let not your heart be troubled. Did you make room for someone? Day six hundred thirty-two.

Philip is the practical one. Back in chapter six, when five thousand hungry people sat on a hillside, Philip was the one who did the math: two hundred pennyworth of bread wouldn't be enough. Now it's the last supper, and Jesus has been talking for a while about going to the Father, about the way, about knowing the Father already. And Philip, still at the table, says what a lot of people have quietly wanted to say. Enough talk. Just show us. One look, and we'll be satisfied. It's a very honest request. Today, the answer he gets.

In the King James Bible Philip says: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us." It sufficeth us: that would do it. And the reply comes with a little ache in it: "Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." Three years of meals and roads and boats, and Philip is still waiting for the real thing to show up. The answer is that it already has. Hold that up against the Hebrew Bible for a moment. Moses once asked to see God's glory, and in Exodus he is told no one can see God's face and live. John's Gospel began on the same note: no man hath seen God at any time, and then, the Son has made him known. So when Philip asks to see, the Gospel's answer is a person at a table. Watch how he washes feet, who he eats with, how he speaks to a grieving sister, and you are looking at what God is like. Christians have built a great deal on this line. Most churches read it alongside their teaching that the Father and the Son are distinct and yet one God, and theologians have spent centuries on exactly how to say that well. You don't need the whole doctrine to feel the turn, though. Philip wants a vision in the sky. He's offered a face across the table. Then Jesus promises he won't leave them orphans. The King James says it this way: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you." Another helper is coming, he says, who will stay with them. That's tomorrow's thread, and the next few days'.
screen: `SHOW US THE FATHER, AND IT'S ENOUGH.`
`SO LONG WITH YOU, AND YOU DON'T KNOW ME?`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD; THE SON MAKES HIM KNOWN.`
then, large: `HE THAT HATH SEEN ME HATH SEEN THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God's face in kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one scene from the Gospels where Jesus is kind. Washing the disciples' feet. Bending down to write in the dirt. Calling a short man down from a tree. Pick one and let it play slowly. Watch his hands. Watch who he looks at. If you're a Christian, this is what the line says God looks like. If you're learning, simply notice what kind of face the Gospel is describing. If you pray, you can hold that scene before God in silence. The bell holds the time.
Show us the Father. Philip's honest request, and the answer: whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father.
Your line: seen the father. Today, when someone is kind to you, pause and notice what that kindness shows you about the one who gave it. Day six hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Christians often read John 14 at funerals and in the weeks after Easter, and many hear in Jesus's reply to Philip the heart of their belief that in Jesus God is made known.

fork.setup: you're Philip. Jesus has been talking for hours about the Father. you want something more solid. what do you say?
options: show us the Father, and that'll be enough.
fork.reveal: Philip asks to be shown, and the answer turns him back to the person in front of him: he that hath seen me hath seen the Father.

original.note: Greek: show us the Father. deixon is a command: point it out, put it in front of us.

trapdoor: what you thought: Philip asks a question he should have known the answer to.
what it means: Philip wants one clear vision of God, and is pointed to the person he's been eating with for years.
what a scholar hears: John opened by saying no one has seen God and the Son has made him known (1:18). Philip's request lets that opening come home.

notes: John 6:7: Philip's 'two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient' (KJV wording paraphrased in the hook). Confirm.
Exodus 33:20 and John 1:18 paraphrased to frame the request. Confirm the framing is fair to the Hebrew Bible and not a contrast against it.
The Trinitarian sentence ('distinct and yet one God') is kept brief and descriptive; non-Trinitarian Christian groups read the verse differently. Keeper may want a line on that.
John 14:16 'another Comforter' is mentioned only as a teaser; the Advocate is taught on day 637.
